# Glossary for The Saints Who Meet Arthur

**Read in:** [UK English](uk/GLOSSARY.md)

The people, places and old words of *The Saints Who Meet Arthur*.

<!-- made-with -->
Translated with machine assistance by Ryan Allen[^ryan-allen] in [Leaftext](https://leaftext.com). More than 3 million new tokens so far on this book; a working translation, not a scholarly edition.

[^ryan-allen]: **Ryan Allen** designs and builds software. Good work disappears into what it's for. [ryanallen.com](https://ryanallen.com) · [GitHub](https://github.com/ryanallen) · [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryanallencom) · [Leaftext](https://leaftext.com)

[^how-designed-the-system]: The tools that made this book, its checks and the rules they hold were designed as one system, and every line in it came out of that system. When a passage reads wrong, the fix goes into the system and the book is made again, never written in by hand, so it reaches every book on the shelf.

[^how-all-checks-passed]: Every range was run through the book's own check tool and the shelf's checks, and nothing was ticked done until they passed: a missing page, a broken link, an old word, a word repeated too soon, a wrong mark and a change nobody logged are all refused.

[^how-readable-first]: Each passage is told the way a good English writer would tell it today, then checked against the source so every event, person and act is there and nothing is invented.

[^how-plain-speech]: No Bible cadence and no stiff old-translation voice: no chains of "and… and… and", no solemn word order, no word nobody says now.

[^how-shaped-for-english]: Each sentence is written as English, not in the source's grammar: a verb rather than a noun made of one, never a clause hanging off a clause, and what someone must do before where or why, with nothing lost. Every sentence that says a common verb twice was read and either rewritten or kept with the reason.

[^how-every-link-said]: Where the source joins a cause and its effect with a bare "and", the English says how they connect, with "to", "by", "so", "until" or "because"; where it strings quotations together, the English says who speaks each one and why, never a bare "Again:".

[^how-nothing-said-twice]: What the source says twice, a doubled verb or a speech the narration has just told, is said once, unless a speaker repeats it on purpose, and the book's account of its text is given once, its edition and scans cited in full only under Sources.

[^how-the-right-word-each-time]: A source word with several senses takes the English its moment needs, never one word everywhere and never the vaguest.

[^how-no-word-worn-out]: No word comes back within forty words of itself, names and the commonest grammar words aside; the second use takes another word or goes.

[^how-modern-idiom]: Old English turns give way to the ones people use now, in how people talk to and about each other as much as in rare words: "pregnant", "said goodbye", "my mom". Every word judged old is kept in the shelf's list, and the check refuses each one.

[^how-us-english]: The reviewed US master uses Merriam-Webster spelling and usage, the article a US reader says, as "an herb", *The Chicago Manual of Style*, and lengths and distances in feet and miles. A later UK edition is made from that master.

[^how-localized-from-us]: After the complete US book has been read and checked, regional editions are built from that text. The UK edition is first. A shared list and a book's locale record give each changed spelling, word, measure and use, so later editions can start from those choices.

[^how-natural-tenses]: The story is told in the simple past wherever the order of events is plain, as English tells it, not in the source's stacked past tenses.

[^how-neutral-tone]: No archaism and no color the source doesn't give, but a hard word stays hard.

[^how-gender-neutral]: Where the source means anyone, the English says "they", "people" or "anyone", never "he" and never a pair of pronouns; a figure the source names keeps the pronoun the source gives.

[^how-no-false-echoes]: No English turn that calls up a better-known story the source doesn't mean: Christ leads Adam and Eve out of hell, never "casts them out", which calls up Eden. An echo the source means stays.

[^how-read-aloud]: Every sentence or line was read aloud and its slack cut with no fact dropped; prose stays in paragraphs, and verse keeps its lines and stanzas, and its beat and rhyme wherever they survive.

[^how-scenes-read-for-movement]: Each whole scene was read for what each speaker wants and where it turns, and the whole book in order, so the dialogue and paragraph breaks carry it; nothing the source doesn't give was added.

[^how-sources-named]: Every reading says whose it is: the scholars who edited the text by name, the printing by its year, the handwritten copy by its own name, and this translation's own work as "this translation", never "we".

[^how-honest-where-unsure]: Where the dictionaries leave a passage open, it's translated as the scholars who edited the text read it, and the doubt is given in an endnote, never smoothed over.

[^how-fiction-called-fiction]: Each book's note opens by saying whether it's fiction or fact, and which parts were made up. A book is fact only when none of it was made up, so a history with any legend in it counts as fiction.

[^how-no-borrowed-wording]: Nothing was translated from Malory's English or any modern translation; they were used only to find where a passage sits in the legend.

[^how-source-over-malory]: Where Malory tells a passage differently, the source is the story and his version goes in a note; where sources are joined into one book, the one written first leads.

[^how-story-headings]: Every heading says what happens in its section, in a short plain sentence, so the headings alone tell the story, without giving away how a fight, a trial, a prophecy or a secret turns out.

[^how-laid-out-for-screens]: Laid out as a modern book read on a screen: a new speaker starts a new paragraph, no paragraph runs past 130 words, and the punctuation is a US book's.

[^how-malory-cross-referenced]: Where Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* tells the same passage, an endnote names his book and chapters; where it doesn't, nothing is said.

[^how-no-guessed-identities]: When a figure might be a better-known person from another book, the glossary says so only where the sources do; it never guesses.

[^how-no-common-words-glossed]: No ordinary English word is a glossary entry, since an entry is underlined on every page of every book that shares the glossary.

[^how-free-with-credit]: Anyone may use this book freely, crediting Ryan Allen, under the CC BY 4.0 license this book gives.

## New in this translation

An entry marked with an asterisk was written for this translation, not taken from Rees or La Borderie.

## Albennoca

Also: Albennoca

A parish of Brittany where Tudona, the sister of Goeznovius and Majan, builds her first chapel. William's legend names it and says no more of where it lay, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Albion

Also: Albidiam

The oldest name of Britain, known to the Greeks and Romans, perhaps from the white cliffs of its south coast. William's legend says Brutus and Corineus called the island Britain once they'd won it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Albion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albion)

## Altgundliu

Also: Altgundliu

The hill where Gwynllyw had his court, which Cadoc's life says took his name, Allt Gwynllyw, "Gwynllyw's Hill." Wikipedia's Gwynllyw places his later hermitage on Stow Hill in Newport, but Cadoc's life doesn't say that this is the same hill.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Angers

Also: Andegavorum

A city of western France on the Maine, near the Loire, the old capital of Anjou. William's legend makes it the eastern limit of the land Conan Meriadoc's Britons won.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers)

## Anglia

Also: Anglia

The place William's legend calls a very old city of Saxony, from which it says the Saxons named themselves and Britain's English. The Angles really came from Angeln, a peninsula on the Baltic coast of Jutland, not a city.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Armorica

Also: Armoricum

The old name of the land in northwest Gaul that became Brittany, from a Celtic word meaning "by the sea." William's legend says Conan Meriadoc crossed into its bay with a great army of Britons.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Armorica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armorica)

## Arthur

Also: Arthurus, Arthuro, Arthuri, Arthurii, Arthurio, Arthurium, Arthurius, Arthur, Arthurum, Arturi, Arturus, Arturum, Arturo

The legendary king of the Britons, who these saints' lives meet as a powerful ruler. Each life sees him differently: a warlord with his companions, a king hunting a monster, a ruler the saints must humble or help. The lives were written centuries after the time they tell of, and none of them is evidence that he lived.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur)

## Barry Island

Also: videlicet Barren

A peninsula on the coast of the Vale of Glamorgan in south Wales, once an island, now part of the town of Barry. Cadoc's life names its harbor as the place a stranger driven back by storm may land and return to Cadoc's sanctuary. Rees's note identifies the life's Barren with Barry Island.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Barry Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Island)

## Bazlananda

Also: Bazlanandam

A river of Brittany that, with the Doena, runs around the parish of Plebs Denarii, where Tudogilus builds his chapel. The tide runs up both rivers. No secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bedivere

Also: Bedguir, Bedwir

One of Arthur's two companions in Cadoc's life, the Bedwyr of the Welsh tales and one of the oldest figures of Arthur's warband. Later romances make him the knight who throws Arthur's sword back into the lake.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Bedivere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedivere)

## Belnoci

Also: Belnoci

A parish of Brittany where Tudona, the sister of Goeznovius and Majan, builds her second chapel. William's legend names it and says no more of where it lay, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Bochriucarn

Also: Bochriucarn

A hill on the border of Brychan's and Gwynllyw's kingdoms, in south Wales, where Brychan's men catch up with Gwynllyw. Cadoc's life gives its Welsh name and translates it, "the jaw of the stone road." Rees thought it lay in the north of Bedwellty parish in Monmouthshire, near the Rhiw Carn road toward Llangynidr.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Britain

Also: Brittannie, Brittanniam, Britaniam, Britanie, Britania

The island of Great Britain, holding today's England, Wales and Scotland. The Welsh lives mean the whole island of the Britons. Goeznovius's legend calls it Greater Britain to set it apart from Lesser Britain, which is Brittany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain)

## Britons

Also: Brittanorum, Brittones, Brittannigenarum, Britannorum, Britani, Britones, Britonibus, Britonum, Bretons

The Celtic people of Britain, the ancestors of the Welsh, the Cornish and the Bretons, who spoke the language Welsh and Breton grew from. Goeznovius's legend counts the settlers of Brittany among them, and Efflamm's life names Brittany's language after them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Celtic Britons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_Britons)

## Brittany

Also: Ulteriorem Britanniam, Britanniam, Britanniæ, minor Britannia, minorem Britaniam, Britanniam minorem

The peninsula of northwest France, the Roman Armorica, settled by Britons from Britain who gave it its name and its language. Efflamm's life calls it simply Britain; Illtud's life calls it Further Britain; Goeznovius's legend says it was named Lesser Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany)

## Brutus

Also: Bruto

The legendary first king of the Britons, a descendant of the Trojan Aeneas, said to have given the Britons their name. William's legend opens its history with him winning the island.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Brutus of Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutus_of_Troy)

## Brychan

Also: Brachanus, Brachano

The legendary king of Brycheiniog in south Wales, remembered as the father of dozens of saints. In Cadoc's life he refuses Gwynllyw's envoys who ask for his daughter Gwladys.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Brychan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brychan)

## Brycheiniog

Also: Brecheniauc

A small kingdom of southeast Wales around today's Brecon, which Cadoc's life says took its name from Brychan, its king. Its border with Gwynllwg runs past the hill Bochriucarn.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Brycheiniog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brycheiniog)

## Cadoc

Also: Cadocus, Cadoci, Cadocum

A Welsh saint of the sixth century, abbot of Llancarfan in south Wales and the son of Gwynllyw and Gwladys. His life, written by Lifris, shows him standing up to Arthur and setting the terms of the sanctuary his monastery gives.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cadoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadoc)

## Cadwy

Also: Cato, Catonem

A ruler who reigns beside Arthur in Carannog's life, holding his court with him at Din Draithou. Wikipedia's Carannog calls him Cadwy, Duke of Cornwall; the life itself says only that he and Arthur ruled there together.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Carannog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carannog)

## Carannog

Also: Carantocus

A Welsh saint of the sixth century, an abbot venerated in Ceredigion, Cornwall, Somerset and Brittany, called Carantoc in English too. His life tells how he set an altar given by Christ adrift on the sea and followed it to Arthur's country.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Carannog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carannog)

## Carhampton

Also: Carrum

A village in west Somerset, near the Bristol Channel coast, about four miles east of Minehead. Carannog's life calls its land Carrum and says a great serpent was laying it waste when Carannog came there.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Carhampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhampton)

## Carrou

Also: Carrou

The church Carannog's life says he built where his altar came ashore the second time, at the mouth of the Guellit, and which it calls the city of Carrou. The life names it and says no more, and no source opened says where it stood or that it's Carhampton, where he built his first church.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Castellum Collobii

Also: Collobii

A fort in Brittany, about two stades from the chapel Majan builds across an arm of the sea from his father's. William's legend names it and says no more, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Castrum Meriadoci

Also: Castrum Meriadoci

"Meriadoc's Castle," the place by the river Guilidona where William's legend says Conan Meriadoc had his first seat in Brittany. The legend says it still had that name in the writer's day, but no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ceredigion

Also: Kerediciaun

A kingdom of west Wales on Cardigan Bay, now a county of Wales. Carannog's life calls it his own country, where he lived in a cave and worked miracles before setting his altar on the sea.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Kingdom of Ceredigion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ceredigion)

## Conan Meriadoc

Also: Conanus Meriadocus, Meriadocus

The legendary founder of Brittany, a Briton who Breton tradition says led settlers across the sea from Britain. William's legend calls him a Catholic and a warrior, who took the land between the two seas as far as Angers.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Conan Meriadoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_Meriadoc)

## Corineus

Also: Corineo

The legendary companion of Brutus, a Trojan war leader strong enough to fight giants, said to have given Cornwall its name. William's legend names him beside Brutus winning the island.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Corineus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corineus)

## Cornwall

Also: Cornubiam

The peninsula at the southwest tip of Britain, a British kingdom in these centuries, whose people spoke Cornish, close to Breton and Welsh. Efflamm's life says his wife Enora went there late in her life to found a house of women. The Latin name could also mean Cornouaille, in the west of Brittany, and the life doesn't say which.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall)

## David

Also: David

Saint David, called Dewi in Welsh, the patron saint of Wales, a bishop and monk of the sixth century who founded the monastery at today's St Davids. In Cadoc's life he's one of the churchmen Cadoc calls to judge between him and Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_David)

## Din Draithou

Also: Dindrarthou

The fort where Carannog's life says Cadwy and Arthur lived, in the country where Carannog's altar came ashore. Wikipedia's Carannog places it at Dunster in Somerset, on the Bristol Channel near Carhampton, though the life itself doesn't say where it lay.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Carannog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carannog)

## Dochdwy

Also: Dochu, Docguinno, Doguuinno

A Welsh saint of the sixth century, remembered as the founder of the monastery at Llandough near Penarth, south of Cardiff. In Cadoc's life he's one of the churchmen who judge between Cadoc and Arthur, and Cadoc gives him an estate.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Doena

Also: Doenam

A river of Brittany that, with the Bazlananda, runs around the parish of Plebs Denarii, where Tudogilus builds his chapel. William's legend says the sea's tides mix with both, but no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Donguel

Also: Donguel

An old cell near the shore, not far from where Efflamm landed, which his life says the Bretons call Donguel and the ancients built. La Borderie discusses it in his commentary but gives no certain place for it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Efflamm

Also: Euflamus, Euflami, Euflamum, Euflamo

A Breton saint of the late fifth or sixth century, said to be the son of an Irish king, remembered at Plestin-les-Grèves on the north coast of Brittany. His life, kept at Tréguier, tells how he left his bride on their wedding night to live as a hermit across the sea.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Efflamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efflamm)

## Eliman

Also: Eliman

The father of Ligessauc, the war leader Arthur pursues in Cadoc's life. The life names him only as Ligessauc's father, and no other source opened tells who he was.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Enora

Also: Honora

Efflamm's wife, the daughter of an Irish king, who his life calls Honora and Breton tradition Enora. Married to him to seal a peace between their fathers, she agrees with him to keep her virginity.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Efflamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efflamm)

## Eudo

Also: Eudoni

The bishop the priest William addresses the legend of Goeznovius, calling him bishop in the twenty-fourth year of his office. Wikipedia's Goeznovius calls him Bishop Eudo of Léon and says no other source knows him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Goeznovius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goeznovius)

## Gaul

Also: Gallie

The Roman land west of the Rhine, roughly today's France and Belgium. William's legend says Conan crossed to the gulf of Armorica in Gaul, and says Arthur won victories in Gaul as well as in Britain.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul)

## Glamorgan

Also: Morcaniensium

The coastal region of south Wales from Cardiff west to Swansea, which as the kingdom of Morgannwg gave its name to the men Illtud's life calls the Morcanienses. Illtud's life makes Poulentus their king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamorgan)

## Glyn Rhosyn

Also: Rosina Valle

The valley in the far southwest of Wales where Saint David founded his monastery, at today's St Davids in Pembrokeshire. Padarn's life gives it in Latin, "the valley of roses," the meaning of its Welsh name.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Goeznovius

Also: Goeznovei, Gocznoveus, Goeznoveus

A Breton saint, called Goueznou in Breton, who his legend says was born in Britain and came to Brittany with his father, his brother and his sister. He's venerated around Brest. His legend opens on a history of the Britons that names Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Goeznovius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goeznovius)

## Guellit

Also: Guellit

The river mouth where Carannog's life says his altar came ashore the second time, in the country of Cadwy and Arthur. The life names it and says no more, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Guilidona

Also: Guilidonam

The river by which William's legend says Conan Meriadoc had his first seat in Brittany, within the bounds of the parish of Plougoulm. The legend names it and says no more, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Gwladys

Also: Guladus, Gladusa

A Welsh saint, the daughter of King Brychan of Brycheiniog and the mother of Saint Cadoc. Cadoc's life describes her as a very beautiful young woman, sitting with her sisters at her father's court when Gwynllyw's men come.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gwladys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwladys)

## Gwynllwg

Also: Gunliauc, Guunliauc

A district of southeast Wales between the Rhymney and the Usk, around today's Newport, which Cadoc's life says took its name from Gwynllyw, its king. Ligessauc hides there with Cadoc.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gwynllwg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwynllwg)

## Gwynllyw

Also: Gundleius, Gundleii, Gundleio

A king of Gwynllwg in southeast Wales, remembered as a warlord who later became a hermit and saint and founded the church at Newport. In Cadoc's life he wants Brychan's daughter Gwladys for his wife and is refused.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Gwynllyw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwynllyw)

## Hyrglas

Also: Hyrglas

The rock on the shore of Brittany where Efflamm's life says his ship put in, which the people of the province call Hyrglas. La Borderie's note identifies it with the Roch-Hirglas, "the long blue rock," at Saint-Michel-en-Grève on the north coast of Brittany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Iestyn

Also: Jestinus, Jestini, Gestine

A Welsh saint of the sixth century, who Efflamm's life calls Jestinus and Breton tradition remembers at Plestin. The life says he lived in Efflamm's cell before him and comes back to it from a pilgrimage to the tombs of the apostles in Rome.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Iestyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Iestyn)

## Illtud

Also: Iltutus

A Welsh saint of the late fifth and early sixth centuries, who founded the monastery and school of Llantwit Major in Glamorgan. His life says he was a Breton, Arthur's cousin, and a soldier before he turned to the Church.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Illtud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illtud)

## Ireland

Also: Hyberniæ

The large island west of Great Britain, across the Irish Sea. Efflamm's life says he was born there to a king, at a time when its people were worn down by war with a neighboring king.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland)

## Irish

Also: Hyberniensis, Hyberniensibus, Hyberniensium, Hybernienses

The people of Ireland, who Efflamm's life shows crying to heaven for an end to their wars. The life says his birth was meant to bring them peace.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Irish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_people)

## Jerusalem

Also: Ierusalem

The holy city of the Jews in Judea, where Christ was crucified and, Christians believe, rose from the dead. Padarn's life says an angel sent David, Padarn and Teilo there to be made bishops.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem)

## Jesus Christ

Also: Christus, Christo, Christi, Christe, Jesus, Jesu

The founder of Christianity, a Jewish teacher of the first century who Christians believe to be the son of Yahweh, who died on the cross and rose again. Carannog's life says Christ gave the saint his altar.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus)

## Kay

Also: Cei, Kei

One of Arthur's two companions in Cadoc's life, the Cai of the Welsh tales and one of the oldest figures of Arthur's warband. Later romances make him Arthur's steward, known for his sharp tongue.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Sir Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Kay)

## Landa

Also: Landa

The place where William's legend says Goeznovius, the last of his family to settle, built his chapel, four miles from the city of the Osismii. It names the chapel there the Peniticium Goeznovei.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Landdeui Pennbei

Also: Landdeui Pennbei

The estate Cadoc gives Saint David after the judgment at the Usk, according to Cadoc's life. Its Welsh name begins with llan, "church," and Dewi, David's Welsh name, but no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Landubrguir

Also: Landubrguir

The estate Cadoc gives Dochdwy after the judgment at the Usk, according to Cadoc's life. Its Welsh name begins with llan, "church," but the life says no more of where it lay, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Léguer

Also: Leguer

A river of northern Brittany that runs through Lannion to the sea. Efflamm's life says Enora came ashore below the city above the Léguer, which La Borderie's note identifies as the Roman fort at Le Yaudet, at the river's mouth.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Ligessauc

Also: Ligessauc, Lauhiir

A war leader of the Britons in Cadoc's life, the son of Eliman, called Lauhiir, which the life translates "Long Hand." He killed three of Arthur's soldiers and could find no one to shelter him until he came to Cadoc.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Maidoc

Also: Maidoc

One of the churchmen Cadoc calls to judge between him and Arthur at the Usk. Cadoc's life names him once and says no more; it doesn't say whether he's Máedóc of Ferns, the Irish saint who studied under David.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Majan

Also: Maianus

The younger son of Tudogilus and brother of Goeznovius, a Breton saint. William's legend says he built his chapel across an arm of the sea from his father's, near the fort of Castellum Collobii.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Ténénan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_T%C3%A9n%C3%A9nan)

## Merthir Tecmed

Also: Merthir Tecmed

The estate Cadoc gives Teilo after the judgment at the Usk, according to Cadoc's life. Its Welsh name begins with merthyr, "a martyr's shrine," but no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Moses

Also: Moyse

The prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt and through the desert, where twice the thirsty people got water from a rock at his prayer. Efflamm calls on that miracle when he prays for water for Arthur.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses)

## Nantes

Also: Nannetensi

A city of western France on the Loire, near its mouth, long the chief city of the south of Brittany. William's legend says Conan Meriadoc's Britons won all its territory.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes)

## Osismii

Also: Ocismorum

A Gallic people of the far west of the Brittany peninsula in Roman times. William's legend measures four miles from their city to Goeznovius's chapel, and La Borderie's note takes that city for Brest.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Osismii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osismii)

## Padarn

Also: Paternus, Paterni, Paternum

A Welsh saint of the early sixth century, an abbot and bishop remembered at Llanbadarn Fawr in Ceredigion. His life says he went to Jerusalem with David and Teilo and came back with a staff and a tunic woven in one piece.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Padarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padarn)

## Pengouet

Also: Pengouet

The name William's legend says the heathen natives of Brittany were called, which it translates "dog heads." The legend calls them heathen to explain why Conan Meriadoc's Britons killed them.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Peniticium Goeznovei

Also: Peniticium

"Goeznovius's place of penance," the name William's legend says the chapel at Landa had in the writer's day. The commune of Gouesnou, near Brest, keeps the saint's name, but the legend doesn't say whether the chapel stood there.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Plebs Denarii

Also: Denarii

The parish where William's legend says Tudogilus built his chapel and lived as a hermit, between the rivers Bazlananda and Doena. The legend names it and says no more, and no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Plestin

Also: Plestina

A town on the north coast of Brittany, today Plestin-les-Grèves, near Lannion. Efflamm's life says the district took its name from Iestyn, and La Borderie's note gives the old form, Plou-Jestin, "Iestyn's parish."<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Plestin-les-Grèves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plestin-les-Gr%C3%A8ves)

## Plougoulm

Also: Plebis Columbe

A parish of Finistère, on the north coast of Brittany, near Saint-Pol-de-Léon. William's legend calls it the Plebs Columbe and puts Conan Meriadoc's first seat within its bounds, and La Borderie's note identifies it with Plougoulm.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Plougoulm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plougoulm)

## Poulentus

Also: Poulentum, Poulento

The king of Glamorgan in Illtud's life, whose household Illtud joins after visiting Arthur, and who makes him master of his soldiers. Wikipedia's Illtud calls him King Poulentus; no other source opened knows him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Illtud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illtud)

## Reneder

Also: Reneder

One of the churchmen Cadoc calls to judge between him and Arthur at the Usk. Cadoc's life names him once and says nothing more, and no source opened tells who he was.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Rennes

Also: Redonico

The chief city of Brittany, on the Vilaine in northwest France, once the city of the Redones, a Gallic people. William's legend says Conan Meriadoc's Britons won all its territory with Nantes's.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes)

## Rithguutebou

Also: Rithguutebou

The ford of the Usk where Cadoc and Arthur argue out the price of Ligessauc's life, according to Cadoc's life. Its Welsh name is often read "the ford of answers," but the life itself doesn't translate it.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## River Thaw

Also: Naudauani

A short river of the Vale of Glamorgan in south Wales, which reaches the Bristol Channel at Aberthaw. Illtud's life says he and his wife camped beside it in summer after he left Poulentus's service. Rees's note on Cadoc's life identifies the Nadauan with the Thaw.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Thaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thaw)

## Saint Peter

Also: Petri

Peter the apostle, the leader of Jesus's twelve followers, who tradition makes the first bishop of Rome, where his tomb is. Efflamm's life says Iestyn comes back from a pilgrimage to the houses of Peter and the other apostles.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter)

## Saxons

Also: Saxones, Saxonum, Saxonibus

One of the Germanic peoples from the North Sea coast, today's northern Germany and Denmark, who settled Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries. William's legend says Vortigern brought them in, Arthur drove them back, and they returned after him.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons)

## Saxony

Also: Saxonie

The homeland of the Saxons in northern Germany, between the Rhine and the Elbe, called Old Saxony to set it apart from the later German state. William's legend says Vortigern called warriors from there.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Old Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Saxony)

## Severn

Also: Sabrinam

The longest river of Britain, flowing from mid Wales out into the Bristol Channel. Carannog's life says he came to it to cross the sea and set his altar on the water.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Severn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Severn)

## Talgarth

Also: Talgarth

A small town in Powys, in the Black Mountains of mid Wales, near Brecon. Cadoc's life says it was the court of King Brychan, where Gwynllyw's men found Gwladys.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Talgarth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talgarth)

## Teilo

Also: Teliauuo, Theleauuo, Teliau

A Welsh saint of the sixth century, a bishop remembered at Llandeilo and Llandaff and a companion of Saint David. In Cadoc's life he judges between Cadoc and Arthur; in Padarn's he travels to Jerusalem.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Teilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Teilo)

## Trefredinauc

Also: Trefredinauc

The place where Cadoc's life says the bundles of fern turned back into cattle in their owners' barns. Its Welsh name means "the fern farm," as the life translates it, but no secure identification of it's known.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

## Trynihid

Also: Trynnihid

Illtud's wife, who travels with him to Poulentus's court and stays with him when he leaves it. Wikipedia's Illtud calls her Trynihid; no other source opened knows her.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Illtud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illtud)

## Tudogilus

Also: Tudogilus

A Briton of free birth who William's legend says left Britain for Brittany with his three children, Goeznovius, Majan and Tudona. Wikipedia's Saint Ténénan names him Saint Tudon and says he may be the same man as Saint Ténénan.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Ténénan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_T%C3%A9n%C3%A9nan)

## Tudona

Also: Tudona

The daughter of Tudogilus and sister of Goeznovius and Majan. William's legend says she chose to live as a nun rather than marry, and built two chapels in Brittany.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Saint Ténénan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_T%C3%A9n%C3%A9nan)

## Usk

Also: Oscam, Osce

The river that runs through southeast Wales to the Severn estuary at Newport. Cadoc's life sets the dispute between Cadoc and Arthur on its two banks.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [River Usk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Usk)

## Venus

Also: Veneris

The Roman goddess of love and beauty. Efflamm's life says he spoke to his bride on their wedding night with chaste words, not the soft words of Venus.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Venus (mythology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_(mythology))

## Vortigern

Also: Vortigernus

The British king who, in legend, invited the Saxons into Britain to defend it and lost much of it to them. William's legend calls him a usurper who held the kingdom unjustly.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Vortigern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortigern)

## William

Also: Guillelmus

The priest who writes the legend of Goeznovius for Bishop Eudo and names himself in its greeting. Wikipedia's Goeznovius calls him a Breton chaplain in the bishop's household and says the legend is now dated to the late twelfth or early thirteenth century, whatever year it claims.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Goeznovius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goeznovius)

## Yahweh

The name of the god of the Israelites, the one god Jews and Christians worship. The Latin of these lives calls it only god or lord, and this translation gives it its name.<sup>[\*](GLOSSARY.md#new-in-this-translation)</sup>

Wikipedia: [Yahweh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh)
